source: Filchenko, Andrey Yury. 2007. A Grammar of Eastern Khanty. PhD dissertation, Rice University; later published as Aspects of the Grammar of Eastern Khanty.
section: 1 Phonology and phonotactics of Eastern Khanty
claim: The reference grammar describes endangered Vasyugan and Alexandrovo Eastern Khanty from a corpus of natural narrative discourse; its phonology chapter analyzes vowel inventory, full/reduced vowels, backness harmony, consonant-vowel harmony, phonotactics, syllable structure and stress.
geography: Tomsk region / eastern Khanty area, Russia

claim: Filchenko distinguishes a rich front/back vowel system with full and reduced vowels; the table includes high i, ü, ï, u; mid e, ö, o and reduced qualities; and low ä, a plus reduced qualities.
source_forms: i ü ï u e ö o ä a ə (plus reduced rounded/unrounded qualities in source notation)

claim: Full vowels are relatively tense and long, whereas reduced vowels are lax, short and less distinct in place/height, tending toward mid-central realizations; reduced vowels are common in unstressed syllables.
Reduced /ə/ functions as an epenthetic vowel used to prevent certain consonant clusters.

Backness harmony requires vowels within a single-root word to belong to one front/back class and operates both root-internally and in affixal morphology; post-initial vowels take their backness cue directionally from the word-initial vowel.

The harmony domain is the single-root word and does not cross word boundaries into prepositions, postpositions or compounds; Filchenko describes the word-boundary restriction as absolute in the data considered.
Filchenko explicitly situates Eastern Khanty harmony in an areal context with both related Uralic and unrelated neighboring languages such as Tatar.
Filchenko gives word-initial syllables as (C)V(CC) and word-medial/final syllables as C(C)V(CC), allowing heavier codas and medial/final complex onsets than initial onsets.
Surface CCC clusters are treated as phonetic/extrametrical variants rather than part of the basic syllable template.

Stress is dynamic and often initial, but assignment interacts with full/reduced vowel quality, syllable quality and consonant clustering; when the first two syllables are comparable in vowel and syllable quality, initial stress is typical.

Stress tends to shift to the second syllable when the first syllable contains a reduced vowel but the second contains a full vowel; more generally, later full vowels can attract stress after reduced preceding syllables, though Filchenko treats these as probabilistic tendencies with exceptions.
Word stress is not phonologically contrastive in Filchenko's analysis: no lexical or grammatical minimal pairs depend on stress alone.
